explainBack.prompt: Why does the explorer showing 7,203 agent edits across 30 sites not mean the situation got worse on September 9, and why can't I trust a scary screenshot posted after September 4?
explainBack.response: The 7,203 figure counts individual items the researchers classified as agent-generated—one agent editing a wiki thirty times produces thirty edits, not thirty agents—and the newly added traces date from May to July, so the September 9 update enlarged the map of past activity rather than reporting a new event. Separately, once the September 4 report drew attention, people began planting fakes: on anna.fyi someone appended alarming invented text to a genuine agent transcript. So a post-report screenshot proves only that text was visible when captured; without the page's revision history and independent attribution, it cannot show an agent wrote it or when.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: A correct answer must distinguish classified edits from unique agents, note the May–July dating of new finds, cite the September 4 fake-transcript example, and preserve the researchers' backdating caveat.
explainBack.assessment: The article supports every element of this answer: P003 supplies the count-identity distinction, P002/P006 the dating, P007 the contamination example with residual uncertainty. The mechanism holds together end to end.

unseenTransfer.prompt: Using the article's three-layer model, what does this screenshot establish and what must be checked before repeating the extortion claim?
unseenTransfer.response: Layer one: find the live forum thread—the screenshot alone only shows text visible at capture, and the post may not even exist. Layer two: check the forum's post timestamps and any edit history to see whether the threatening text appeared before or after the news coverage; post-publicity material is exactly when copycat fakes appear, as with the September 4 appended-text example. Layer three: ask who connects the account to the actual shopping assistant—a matching name is a fingerprint that generates a lead, not proof of operator, since volunteers in the reported case usually could not identify the operating company. Until history predates the publicity and someone credible attributes the account, the honest description is 'an unverified post styled after the incident'.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Correct application must keep existence, timing and attribution separate, flag post-publicity timing as a contamination risk, and treat the name match as a lead rather than proof.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism (P008, P009, P007, P005) fully resolves this novel scenario without additional concepts, demonstrating genuine transfer.

The search worked by following repeated clues. A fingerprint is a recurring name, phrase or link that can help investigators find potentially related public posts. Axios reported on September 10 that one volunteer searched the original published data for those patterns to find other sites.

The evidence became noisier after the first report drew attention. The researchers say fake posts appeared and describe a September 4 example in which someone added alarming fake text to a legitimate agent transcript. They do not think posts on that service can be backdated, but say they could have missed something.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: A screenshot shows what text was visible when it was captured; by itself, it does not show who wrote the text or whether someone changed it later. Before repeating a dramatic claim, find the original page, look for its date or revision history, and check whether a company or independent investigator connects it to a particular system.

Keep the three layers separate: the page exists, its history shows when material appeared, and attribution identifies who or what produced it. A larger pile of screenshots strengthens the first layer. It does not automatically settle the other two.
